newsitem.title: USA: Fed seen hiking rates in second half '97--U.S. PSA.
newsitem.headline: Fed seen hiking rates in second half '97--U.S. PSA.

text.p: Robust U.S. economic growth in the second half of 1997 should prompt the Federal Reserve to raise short-term interest rates before the end of the year, said PSA The Bond Market Association in its annual midyear economic forecast released Wednesday.
The views of PSA's 11-member economic advisory committee differed as to how much strength the economy would exhibit and how much Fed tightening would be needed.
On average, the committee predicted the federal funds rate would rise to 6.0 percent from its current 5.50 percent.
They did unanimously agree, however, that the Fed would not raise interest rates at its upcoming Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting in July.
A minority of members said that future tightening was warranted despite the relatively benign picture.

"These members see the recent indicators of slowing growth as temporary and regard the levels of labor utilization -- the 4.8-percent May unemployment rate -- as signaling increases in wage pressures with the potential to aggravate inflation," it said.
An anticipated rise in short-term interest rates should push the 30-year bond yield just above 7.0 percent by year end, according to a majority of members.

Looking at macroeconomic indicators, the committee forecast year-end to year-end growth in 1997 at an average 3.4 percent; Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth will reach 2.8 percent in the second half of 1997, and the year-end to year-end inflation as measured by the Consumer Price Index (CPI) was expected to slow to 2.4 percent from 3.2 percent in 1996.
Turning to fiscal policy, the committee forecast a $70 billion budget deficit for fiscal 1997, down from $107 billion.
Along with the budget agreement, deficit reduction was expected to have a positive effect on U.S. capital markets, PSA said.
"U.S. financial markets are well positioned as foreign institutional investors continue to maintain large holdings of dollar-denominated fixed income securities," it said.
In addition, members of the committee were polled on whether the scheduled January 1999 introduction of the euro was expected to be met.
